quote: Hängen die Ergebnisse vielleicht mit der rationalen Transformation zusammen, wo ja auch ein solcher Multiplikator eine Rolle spielt.
english: Are the results perhaps connected with rational transformation, where such a multiplier also plays a role?
topic: A list of research notes: upper bounds for the coefficients of the characteristic function following Noether, representations of a multiple of a ternary form as a sum of three squares, counting contact curves via Abelian functions, and finiteness of integral invariants of an integral linear substitution.

triage.modern_statement: Taken in context, Hilbert seems to be asking whether his results on writing a multiple q·f of a ternary form f as a sum of three squares, where q is an auxiliary 'multiplier' form (this ties in with his count of contact curves via Abelian functions), are structurally connected to the theory of rational transformations, probably the transformation of elliptic or Abelian functions, where a 'multiplier' also appears. The note does not say which results it means or which kind of 'rational transformation', so this cannot be stated as a precise mathematical question.
triage.answered_by: No one, as far as I could find. Related work exists: Hilbert himself (1888, ternary quartics as sums of three squares; 1893, Acta Math. 17, a multiplier q such that p·q is a sum of squares); Powers, Reznick, Scheiderer and Sottile (a general ternary quartic has exactly 63 representations as a sum of three squares over C); Plaumann, Sturmfels and Vinzant (who matched these 63 representations to Steiner complexes of bitangents). None of these sources addresses the specific link to 'rational transformation' with a multiplier.

evidence.claim: In 1893 Hilbert showed that for a nonnegative ternary form p there is a nonnegative form q of degree 2d-4 such that p·q is a sum of squares. This is the 'multiplier' result the page context appears to refer to.

Powers, Reznick, Scheiderer and Sottile showed that a general ternary quartic is a sum of three squares in exactly 63 essentially different ways over C. This links sums of three squares to contact curves and bitangents of the quartic.

Plaumann, Sturmfels and Vinzant identify sums of three squares with Steiner complexes of bitangents and compute all 63 Gram matrices. This is the modern algebro-geometric explanation of the count that Hilbert approached through Abelian functions.
A survey describes Hilbert's 1888 proof that a nonnegative ternary quartic is a sum of three squares, and later work on it by Scheiderer and others.

triage.why: The note is a short speculative aside. It never says which 'results' it means or which theory of 'rational transformation' (for example, transformation of Abelian or elliptic functions, or birational transformations). That makes it impossible to turn into a definite problem. The surrounding topics (multipliers for sums of squares, 63 representations of a ternary quartic, contact curves) are well studied and still active in real algebraic geometry. The 63-representation count matches the 2^6−1 = 63 nonzero 2-torsion points of the Jacobian of a genus-3 curve, which hints at a link to Abelian function theory. Still, I found no source that takes up or settles Hilbert's suggested connection to rational transformation. It is not one of his published problems.
